content: Azithromycin is an oral macrolide antibacterial agent approved by the FDA for treating sexually transmitted diseases, mycobacterial infections, community-acquired pneumonia, and pelvic inflammatory disease. Common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain, and vomiting. For adults, the recommended dosage for non-gonococcal urethritis and cervicitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis is a single 1-gram dose. For preventing disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) infections, the recommended dose is 1200 mg once weekly, which may be combined with rifabutin. For treating disseminated MAC infections, a daily dose of 600 mg of azithromycin is recommended, combined with ethambutol at 15 mg/kg daily. Additional antimycobacterial drugs may be added at the discretion of the healthcare provider. For community-acquired pneumonia, the recommended dose is 500 mg intravenously once daily for at least two days, followed by 500 mg orally once daily to complete a 7-10 day course. For pelvic inflammatory disease, the dose is 500 mg intravenously once daily for 1-2 days, followed by 250 mg orally once daily to complete a 7-day course. If anaerobic microorganisms are suspected, an additional antimicrobial agent with anaerobic activity should be used. Off-label adult uses include azithromycin 500 mg orally once daily for at least three months or a single 1-gram dose for certain conditions. Pediatric use is limited, with some off-label uses supported by guidelines, such as 15 mg/kg orally for specific infections. Azithromycin is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to macrolides or ketolides and those with a history of cholestatic jaundice or hepatic dysfunction associated with prior azithromycin use. Warnings include the potential for serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, which may recur after discontinuation of symptomatic treatment. Hepatotoxicity, including liver failure, has been reported, and the drug should be discontinued if signs of hepatitis occur. Azithromycin may prolong the QT interval, increasing the risk of arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes, particularly in at-risk populations (e.g., those with congenital long QT syndrome, bradyarrhythmias, or electrolyte imbalances). Clostridium difficile-associated diarrhea (CDAD) has been reported and may range from mild to fatal colitis. Azithromycin may exacerbate symptoms of myasthenia gravis. Adverse reactions observed in clinical trials were generally mild to moderate and reversible upon discontinuation. The most common reactions in adults included diarrhea, nausea, and abdominal pain. Chronic therapy for MAC prevention in immunocompromised HIV patients showed similar adverse reactions to short-term regimens, with reversible hearing impairment reported in some cases. Drug interactions include increased azithromycin serum concentrations when co-administered with nelfinavir, requiring close monitoring for adverse effects. Concomitant use with warfarin may potentiate anticoagulant effects, necessitating careful monitoring of prothrombin time. Potential interactions with other macrolides, digoxin, and phenytoin warrant caution. Azithromycin is excreted in breast milk in small amounts, and caution is advised when administered to nursing mothers. Its safety and efficacy in pediatric HIV patients for MAC prevention or treatment have not been established. Elderly patients may be more susceptible to QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. Azithromycin acts by binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit of susceptible microorganisms, inhibiting protein synthesis. It concentrates in phagocytes and fibroblasts, contributing to its distribution to inflamed tissues. The drug's pharmacokinetics include extensive tissue distribution and a prolonged half-life due to tissue uptake and release.
